articles.title: Neotenic expansion of adult-born dentate granule cells reconfigures GABAergic inhibition to enhance social memory consolidation
articles.authors: Ain Chung, Jason Bondoc Alipio, Megha Ghosh
articles.abstract: Adult-born dentate granule cells (abDGCs) contribute to hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG)-CA3/CA2 circuit functions in memory encoding, retrieval and consolidation. Heightened synaptic and structural plasticity of immature abDGCs is thought to govern their distinct contributions to circuit and network mechanisms of hippocampal-dependent memory operations. Protracted maturation or neoteny of abDGCs in higher mammals is hypothesized to offset decline in adult hippocampal neurogenesis by expanding the capacity for circuit and network plasticity underlying different memory operations. Here, we provide evidence for this hypothesis by genetically modelling the effective impact of neoteny of abDGCs on circuitry, network properties and social cognition in mice. We show that selective synchronous expansion of a single cohort of 4 weeks old immature, but not 8 weeks old mature abDGCs, increases functional recruitment of fast spiking parvalbumin expressing inhibitory interneurons (PV INs) in CA3/CA2, number of PV IN-CA3/CA2 synapses, and GABAergic inhibition of CA3/CA2. This transient increase in feed-forward inhibition in DG-CA2 decreased social memory interference and enhanced social memory consolidation. In vivo local field potential recordings revealed that the expansion of a single cohort of 4-week-old abDGCs increased baseline power, amplitude, and duration, as well as sensitivity to social investigation-dependent rate changes of sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) in CA1 and CA2, a neural substrate for memory consolidation. Inhibitory neuron-targeted chemogenetic manipulations implicate CA3/CA2 INs, including PV INs, as necessary and sufficient for social memory consolidation following neotenic expansion of the abDGC population and in wild-type mice, respectively. These studies suggest that neoteny of abDGCs may represent an evolutionary adaptation to support cognition by reconfiguring PV IN-CA3/CA2 circuitry and emergent network properties underlying memory consolidation.

articles.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference
articles.authors: Deng Pan, Simone D’Ambrogio, Naomi Kingston
articles.abstract: When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

articles.title: JEPA Dots: Dual-Latent World Model for Language-Guided Robot Control
articles.authors: Xianhao Pan, Chi Li, Hongru Li
articles.abstract: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations. To address this challenge, we introduce JEPA Dots (Dynamics-Oriented Task Separation), a compact dual-latent framework that jointly learns visual dynamics and language-guided control through separate dynamics and task representations. Language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention restricts world prediction to instruction-independent dynamics history and supplied actions. In closed-loop evaluation on 40 trained LIBERO tasks, JEPA Dots achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters, compared with the published 78.7% of NanoVLA-S with 161.0M parameters under a different evaluation protocol. In the reference experiment, JEPA Dots also improves overall success from 76.0% for our task-ID-conditioned adaptation baseline to 84.9%, with LIBERO-Goal success increasing from 67.1% to 88.5%. Instruction-switching experiments further confirm that task representations and policy outputs respond to language changes, while dynamics representations and world predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and supplied actions.

articles.title: Episodic memory consolidation by reactivation of human concept neurons during sleep reflects contents, not sequence of events
articles.authors: Johannes Niediek, Thomas Peter Reber, Marcel Bausch
articles.abstract: How do our brains manage to store our everyday experiences into memory? Neurons in the human temporal lobe that respond to the concept of an individual person or object have been shown to provide the semantic building blocks for episodic memory. Recording from 1415 neurons in neurosurgical patients who learned a story involving specific concepts, we found reactivation of neurons representing these concepts during slow-wave sleep after learning. Concept neurons were conjointly reactivated, particularly during sharp-wave ripples, with time lags suitable for synaptic modification. However, the temporal sequence of reactivation did not reflect the sequence of concepts in the learned story. Unlike rodent place cells, which can acquire preferred firing locations during exploration of new environments according to their pre-existing preferred sequence of activation, human concept neurons are tuned to specific semantic contents before learning starts. Consequently, pre-existing firing sequences correlate with consecutive place fields in rodents, but not with sequences of events in human experience. Thus, in contrast to reactivation of rodent place cells, reactivation of human concept cells does not reflect sequences of events in human experience.

articles.title: Human Centric Embodied Intelligence for Soft Wearable Robotics
articles.authors: Rainier F. Natividad, Chen‐Hua Yeow
articles.abstract: Soft wearable robots have evolved rapidly from proof‐of‐concept devices into promising platforms for rehabilitation, occupational assistance, and human augmentation. As the field matures, its central challenge extends beyond developing softer materials and more capable actuators to integrating sensing, intelligence, and human adaptation into systems that users can wear comfortably, trust, and benefit from over long periods. This transition motivates the concept of human centric embodied intelligence (HCEI). In HCEI, intelligence emerges from the coupled human–robot system, through the interaction of morphology, multimodal sensing, adaptive cognition, compliant actuation, and the wearer's own physiological and behavioral adaptation. To organize this perspective, we introduce the perception–cognition–actuation–augmentation (PCAA) framework. It proposes that design start from the augmentation objective, the change sought in the wearer's function, and that the requirements on perception, cognition, and actuation be derived from that objective rather than from the actuating mechanism. Using this framework, we review advances in soft materials, wearable sensing, artificial intelligence, actuation, human–robot interaction, digital twins, clinical translation, manufacturing, regulation, and ethics, and trace how these interdependent components together shape long‐term personalization and real‐world deployment. The review aims to guide future research, encourage interdisciplinary collaboration, and speed the translation of soft wearable robots toward personalized, predictive, and human‐centric wearable intelligence.

articles.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
articles.authors: Jing Liu, Xianhui He, Can Yang
articles.abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity-brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay-in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal-neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

articles.title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"
articles.authors: Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun, Kerda Varaku
articles.abstract: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.

articles.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
articles.authors: Yuzhi Huang, Jie Wu, Fanding Huang
articles.abstract: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

articles.title: Skill-JEPA: Learning Planner-Aligned Action Spaces for World Models
articles.authors: Tomás Couso Coddou, Christ Devia, Rex G. Liu
articles.abstract: World models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn from pixels to predict the outcome of actions in a latent space. To reach a goal, a planner samples many candidate action sequences, uses the model to predict where each one leads, and executes the best one. However, standard planners draw their candidates from a Gaussian, while the model has only seen the structured, state-dependent actions of its training data. Its predictions for such candidates are unreliable, and planning fails more often as goals move farther away. We propose Skill-JEPA, which learns an action space aligned with the planner. A variational autoencoder conditioned on the current state encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a standard Gaussian prior, and decodes them back into actions. The world model predicts the effect of skills rather than raw actions, and the planner searches over skills starting from that same Gaussian, so its candidates resemble the model's training data. Skill-JEPA adds a single module, trained end-to-end with the world model, and leaves the planner untouched, with no subgoals, hierarchy, or hand-designed skills. Across three JEPA world models and four benchmarks, average success on goals 80 steps away rises from 42% with raw actions to 62%; the gains grow with goal distance and hold across four planners. On AntMaze, a quadruped locomotion task, success on goals two maze cells away rises from 0.4% to 38%. This suggests that part of the difficulty of reaching distant goals lies in the action space, and can be removed without changing the planner.

articles.title: RECLAIM: Robot-Vision-Informed Adversarial Patch Defense via Embodied Attention Feedback
articles.authors: Jiayou Zhu, Peng Guo, Litian Zhang
articles.abstract: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.

articles.title: WM-Quant: Rollout-Aware Post-Training Quantization for JEPA-Style World Models
articles.authors: William Hammer, Andy Heuer, Nikhil Krishna
articles.abstract: We present WM-Quant, to our knowledge, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) framework designed specifically for JEPA-style world models. Although world models typically feature relatively few parameters, action planning algorithms often require thousands of inferences, which can quickly become computationally expensive. PTQ is a natural way to reduce this cost. However, we show that in world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error can compound with each predictor step, resulting in action rankings from the quantized model becoming near-random. WM-Quant addresses this with three components that build on existing PTQ methods: early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling. Early-encoder precision protects accurate latent state and goal information to mitigate long-term error propagation. Control-path preservation allows the world model predictor to distinguish between fine-grained actions, significantly improving action rankings and execution. Rollout-aware scaling jointly calibrates encoder and per-step predictor activation ranges with respect to an entire rollout rather than a single prediction, reducing the cumulative rollout error. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves planning success at low bit-widths, approaching full-precision performance at W4A4.

articles.title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models
articles.authors: Yao Zhang, Bin Yu, Shijie Lian
articles.abstract: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.

articles.title: Neuromorphic self-aware wings for embodied-intelligent bionic flying microrobotics
articles.authors: Hao Zheng, Xu Zeng, Yao Tan
articles.abstract: Flying insects achieve robust proprioception and agile flight control using distributed mechanoreceptors on their wings, but current bionic flying microrobots rely heavily on external sensors for state monitoring. Typical sensing solutions including offboard vision or surface-mounted devices inevitably sacrifice either flight autonomy or payload capacity. Inspired by insect wing mechanoreception, we introduce an embodied neuromorphic self-sensing paradigm that eliminates this tradeoff by enabling intrinsic, aerodynamics-maintenance proprioception in flapping-wing systems. Instead of treating the wing solely as a propulsive structure, we reengineer it into a self-contained sensory organ capable of autonomous motion monitoring and health state awareness. We develop an interface charge field mapping model that decouples complex local wing motions, enabling dynamic three-dimensional reconstruction of wing deformation. Building on this theoretical foundation, a conformal bionic mechanoreceptor is directly grown on the wing surface via layered sensitive units. By synergistically combining physics-driven kinematic feature extraction with machine learning, the system achieves real-time fault diagnosis and closed-loop aerodynamic-loss compensation. We do not add sensors to the wing, we make the wing itself the sensory organ. This embodied self-sensing paradigm establishes a new principle for structural intelligence in bionic robotics, offering a promising path toward autonomous, self-aware, and robust miniature flying systems.

articles.title: Connectomes as Structural Priors for Embodied Control: Lessons from Digital Drosophila
articles.authors: Wenxiang Jiang, Lihong Xu
articles.abstract: Synapse-resolved connectomes of Drosophila melanogaster now map the entire adult brain and ventral nerve cord, but behavior also depends on synaptic strengths, neural dynamics, and the body. A connectome is therefore better used as a testable structural prior than as a blueprint to copy. This review examines how digital Drosophila (connectomes plus the models and body simulators built on them) can serve this role in embodied control. We trace how electron-microscopy images become a connectivity graph, where errors enter, and how heterogeneous datasets can be combined reproducibly. We then compare three uses of the graph (extracting a circuit principle, embedding a reconstructed module, or adopting the whole connectome as controller topology) with one another and with conventional controllers, separating experimentally validated findings from computational predictions. Connectome-constrained models can predict neural activity and sensorimotor pathways, but simulated success does not by itself establish biological accuracy, and sensory encoding, motor decoding, and body mechanics are as much part of the controller as the wiring. From this synthesis we derive five candidate design principles (sparse modular communication, recurrent state estimation, hierarchical motor control, selective plasticity, and body–controller co-design) and one methodological principle (anatomically indexed intervention), each paired with falsifiable predictions, matched baselines, and sim-to-real stress tests.

articles.title: Editorial: Neuroadaptive brain-computer interface-driven robotic system for hand rehabilitation in stroke patients
articles.authors: Kai Guo
articles.abstract: Upper-limb dysfunction following stroke remains one of the most persistent sequelae limiting patients' ability to regain independent living, with recovery of distal hand function being particularly challenging. This difficulty arises because grasping, pinching, and fine object manipulation depend heavily on coordinated motor planning, the integrity of residual descending motor pathways, accurate proprioceptive feedback, and sustained, task-specific rehabilitation training.Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and rehabilitation robotic technologies offer complementary strategies for overcoming these clinical limitations. BCIs can directly decode motor intentions from cortical activity even when voluntary movement is severely impaired, whereas peripheral effector devices, such as rehabilitation robots, can translate the decoded motor intentions into timely and precise movement assistance while simultaneously providing task-matched sensory feedback.Accordingly, the central objective of this Research Topic is not merely to automate rehabilitation training, but rather to move toward adaptive closed-loop systems that respond to individual patient states. Such a system is intended to achieve tight coupling and bidirectional interaction among motor-intention decoding, external movement assistance, multimodal sensory feedback, and potentially activity-dependent neuroplasticity; the latter cannot be inferred from feedback alone.The five articles collected in this Research Topic examine this concept from complementary perspectives, including evidence synthesis, randomized clinical evaluation, neurophysiological assessment, and methodological optimization. Together, they address clinical outcomes, the role of contingent feedback, and opportunities for patient-specific rehabilitation.Assistive BCIs compensate for lost function, whereas restorative BCIs aim to facilitate recovery through intention-contingent sensorimotor feedback and activity-dependent plasticity [1]. These approaches may be complementary, particularly for severely affected patients who need assistance to perform meaningful tasks. However, feedback-related clinical gains alone do not prove neuroplastic reorganization. EEG-triggered robotic assistance provides brain-contingent control. More advanced neuroadaptive rehabilitation additionally adjusts assistance, feedback, or task difficulty according to changing neural or behavioral states [2,3]. Continuous individualized adaptation remains a future objective rather than a demonstrated capability of all the systems discussed here.Wang et al., in a meta-analysis of 13 studies involving 488 patients, broaden the scope of robot-assisted rehabilitation beyond motor impairment. Robot-assisted training was associated with improvement in Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores, although sensitivity analyses indicated instability in several cognitive outcomes and the overall quality of evidence was limited. These findings are relevant to neuroadaptive rehabilitation because attention, cognition, and task engagement may influence motor learning and a patient's ability to interact effectively with BCI-robotic systems. This synthesis concerns robotic training without BCI control and cannot establish the effects of brain-contingent rehabilitation.At the motor-function level, Zheng et al. synthesized 27 randomized controlled trials and reported improvements in both upper-and lower-limb Fugl-Meyer scores following BCI-based rehabilitation. Their subgroup analyses further suggested that outcomes may vary with feedback modality, stroke stage, and training intensity. This reinforces an important principle: BCI rehabilitation should not be treated as a single homogeneous intervention, because clinical effects depend on how motor intention is decoded and how feedback is delivered. Considerable between-study heterogeneity limits the interpretation and generalizability of pooled estimates. This principle is directly examined by Jin et al. in an assessor-blinded randomized pilot trial involving 40 patients with subacute stroke. Participants received either EEG-contingent closed-loop motor imagery BCI training with a soft rehabilitation glove or dose-matched motor imagery training with non-EEG-contingent glove assistance. The closed-loop BCI group showed greater improvements in FMA-UE, ARAT, and MBI scores, while exploratory EEG analyses identified changes in alpha-and beta-band sensorimotor activity. Importantly, the active control condition matched motor imagery practice, robotic exposure, training duration, and multisensory feedback, allowing a more focused evaluation of the contribution of EEG-contingent closed-loop control. articles.title: Embodied Graph: A Relational World Model for Long-Horizon Tasks
articles.authors: Zongyuan Wu, Xin Wang, Tongtong Feng
articles.abstract: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.

articles.title: Mechanisms and Applications of Neuroplasticity in Cognitive Enhancement Driven by Brain-Computer Interfaces
articles.authors: Ziwei Dai
articles.abstract: Brain computer interface (BCI) is changing from "reading brain" to "regulating brain". Cognitive enhancement has become an important development direction of BCI, and neural plasticity is the core mechanism connecting BCI intervention and cognitive function improvement. Focusing on the evidence chain of "BCI neural plasticity cognitive enhancement", this paper systematically combines the mechanism of closed-loop neural feedback inducing neural oscillation and synaptic plasticity, and reviews its application in the clinical rehabilitation of AD/MCI, the early intervention of healthy aging and MCI, and the emotional assistance of severe cognitive impairment. Existing studies have provided imaging, behavioral electrophysiology and mediating causal evidence respectively, but there is still a lack of research to verify the three at the same time in the same paradigm, and there are problems such as the timeliness of cognitive state decoding, feedback synchronization, individual differences, standardization of training protocols, long-term safety and cognitive transfer. Cognitive enhanced BCI may also cause social equity and ideological privacy risks. In the future, large sample randomized controlled trials should be carried out to promote the development of personalized, multimodal and family-based BCI systems, and long-term safety assessment, cost control and neural privacy legislation should be strengthened.

articles.title: Expanded States of Consciousness as a Framework for Understanding End-of-Life Experiences in Practice
articles.authors: Ana Cláudia Mesquita Garcia, João Marcos Martins Ferreira, Geovanna Maria Isidoro
articles.venue: Journal of Social Work in End-of-Life & Palliative Care
articles.abstract: End-of-life experiences (EoLEs), including visions, symbolic dreams, sensed presences, meaningful coincidences, and terminal lucidity, have been increasingly recognized in the literature as relevant phenomena in the dying process. However, in clinical practice, these experiences are often interpreted as pathological symptoms, which may limit communication and person-centered care. This article draws on relevant literature on EoLEs and ESCs to examine how these experiences may be understood beyond automatic pathologization and to discuss the implications of this perspective for end-of-life practice. The literature suggests that EoLEs are often experienced as meaningful, comforting, and spiritually significant by patients and families. At the same time, pathologizing interpretations may reduce these experiences to hallucinations, delirium, or other neuropsychiatric symptoms, overlooking their existential, relational, and spiritual dimensions. Interpreting EoLEs through the lens of ESCs offers an alternative framework that may help professionals approach these experiences with greater openness while preserving clinical discernment. This perspective may support more sensitive, person-centered, and spiritually informed end-of-life care, while helping clinicians avoid automatic pathologization, improve communication, and better integrate patients' subjective experiences into care. The ESC framework proposed here is not intended as a definitive explanatory model, but as a possible interpretive lens through which EoLEs may be understood beyond automatic pathological reduction.

articles.title: Reinforced hippocampus-accumbens pathway marks a shift toward cognitive decline in aging
articles.authors: Aurore Ribera, Brenda Fernandes-Dias, Larissa Yugay
articles.abstract: Aging triggers early functional alterations in brain circuits preceding cognitive impairment, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unaddressed. Spatial navigation and memory, among the earliest affected, depend on the hippocampus and downstream targets such as the nucleus accumbens (NAc), which integrates spatial and motivational information to guide goal-directed behaviors. Here we identify age-related, sex-dependent changes in the dorsal hippocampus-NAc (dHPC→NAc) pathway. Combining optogenetics with electrophysiology, chemogenetics, and behavioral analyses in mice, we show that aging shifts the excitation-inhibition balance in dorsal CA1 toward pyramidal neuron hyperactivity, strengthening hippocampal outputs. This selectively enhances synaptic drive onto D1 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons and involves a previously unrecognized long-range parvalbumin-expressing projection. Chemogenetically reducing the dHPC→NAc activity improves memory in aged mice. In humans, fMRI reveals heightened posterior hippocampal activity and stronger posterior HPC-NAc coupling during navigation. Together, we uncover a targetable pathway acting in an intervention-sensitive window of aging to correct negative cognitive trajectories.

articles.title: Frequency-dependent entorhinal cortex stimulation differentially modulates spatial working memory and CA1 network dynamics
articles.authors: Liuxindai Zhang, Qingyun Li, Zhou Xingmin
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT: Entorhinal cortex deep brain stimulation is a promising approach for modulating memory circuits; however, how stimulation frequencies across different frequency bands shape task-relevant hippocampal dynamics and working memory remains unclear. In this study, C57BL/6J mice were implanted with entorhinal cortex stimulation and CA1 recording electrodes and trained in a delayed T-maze spatial working memory task. Entorhinal cortex deep brain stimulation was delivered at 15, 50, or 130 Hz using an intermittent 30-minute protocol before behavioral testing, with a sham-control group. CA1 local field potentials and spiking activity were recorded during the T-maze task. We analyzed oscillatory power, theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and spike-local field potential phase-locking in putative pyramidal neurons and interneurons. Post-mortem immunohistochemistry was used to quantify the excitatory synaptic marker vesicular glutamate transporter 1 expression and the inhibitory marker glutamate decarboxylase 67. Baseline performance was balanced across groups. Within-subject comparisons showed that 15 Hz entorhinal cortex deep brain stimulation significantly improved choice accuracy without altering decision latency. This behavioral improvement was accompanied by increased CA1 theta-, low-gamma-, and high- gamma-band power, enhanced firing and theta-phase locking in putative interneurons, and increased postmortem vesicular glutamate transporter 1 expression density. In contrast, 50 Hz stimulation did not improve choice accuracy and produced divergent cell-type-specific changes in phase-locking, including enhanced theta-locking in putative interneurons but reduced theta-locking in putative pyramidal neurons. Although 130 Hz stimulation increased theta-high- gamma phase-amplitude coupling and GAD67 expression, it did not significantly improve choice accuracy. Sham-operated animals showed no significant behavioral improvement across repeated testing sessions. The frequency of entorhinal cortex deep brain stimulation determined distinct behavioral, electrophysiological, and histological profiles during delayed spatial working memory. The 15-Hz protocol produced the only coherent profile, characterized by improved memory performance accompanied by enhanced CA1 theta/gamma oscillations, increased interneuron theta-phase locking and excitatory synaptic marker density than those observed with the 50- or 130-Hz protocols. These findings indicate that stimulation frequency is a critical determinant of entorhinal cortex-targeted memory modulation.

articles.title: Brain-computer interfaces in acupuncture research: current evidence and methodological challenges
articles.authors: Jinhuan Zhang, Bin Yan, Yu Yang
articles.abstract: Background Despite marked interindividual variability in acupuncture response, most neuroimaging studies remain confined to group-level analyses, offering little practical guidance during treatment. This critical narrative review explores how brain–computer interface (BCI) methods could enable individualized acupuncture and bridge the translational gap between measuring neural responses and using them to inform clinical decision-making. Methods We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore for relevant publications from inception to September 2026. We critically synthesized evidence on acupuncture-related neural responses, state decoding, and outcome prediction, alongside relevant BCI methods. Acupuncture-specific findings were distinguished from general BCI methodology and proposed applications. Studies were examined according to how neural information was used, rather than the recording modality or reported model accuracy. Results EEG and neuroimaging studies demonstrate that acupuncture-related brain responses can be measured. Some models also identify stimulation states or predict clinical outcomes offline. However, these findings do not establish that the identified features are therapeutic targets or that adapting acupuncture to them improves outcomes. We propose a five-level framework encompassing response observation (L0), characterization over time (L1), individual decoding or prediction (L2), prospective decision support or BCI-assisted care (L3), and adaptive closed-loop acupuncture (L4). The reviewed studies do not establish superior clinical outcomes from real-time, neural-state-guided acupuncture compared with standardized open-loop care. Conclusion Neural measurement and prediction provide a foundation for individualized acupuncture, but the clinical benefit of feedback-guided treatment remains unproven. The L0–L4 framework clarifies the evidence needed to advance acupuncture–brain interfaces. Translation requires reproducible neural markers, independent validation, and prospective trials evaluating clinical benefit, with stimulation adjusted within predefined limits under clinician oversight.

articles.title: Circuit mechanisms shaping place-cell and grid-cell representations under environmental deformation
articles.authors: Zhiguang Xu, Boyuan Li, Fei Liu
articles.abstract: Place cells (PCs) in the hippocampus and grid cells (GCs) in the medial entorhinal cortex jointly support spatial representations; however, how interactions between these populations shape representational changes following environmental deformation remains unclear. We developed a biologically grounded circuit model that integrates boundary vector cells, PCs, and modular GC networks through plastic boundary-to-place, place-to-grid, and grid-to-place projections. During initial exposure to compressed or elongated enclosures, GCs exhibited module-dependent grid rescaling and boundary-conditioned phase shifts, whereas PCs showed heterogeneous changes in place-field size and position. Transfer-entropy analysis revealed movement-dependent and boundary-axis-dependent shifts in the directional balance of predictive dependence between PC and GC populations relative to the familiar baseline. During departure, this balance shifted toward grid-to-place and place-to-grid predictive dependence along the deformed and undeformed axes, respectively. With repeated familiarization, different representational features followed distinct, geometry-dependent trajectories rather than uniformly reverting to their familiar-environment configurations. Selective blockade of plasticity in individual pathways revealed distinct effects on familiarization: place-to-grid plasticity supported grid-scale recovery and gains in spatial information, boundary-to-place plasticity modestly promoted grid-scale recovery, and grid-to-place plasticity helped constrain rescaling overshoot. Together, these findings suggest that environmental deformation elicits a multidimensional reorganization of spatial representations, shaped by dynamic place–grid interactions and pathway-specific plasticity, rather than a single uniform transformation.

articles.title: Brain-Inspired Graph Learning: From Neural Connectivity and Spiking Dynamics to Cognitive Plasticity
articles.authors: Chunxiao Yin, Xinyue Zhou, Jing Zhang
articles.abstract: Graph learning provides a framework for modeling relational data, while brain-inspired approaches introduce principles of neural connectivity, neuronal dynamics, synaptic plasticity, and memory into graph-based computation. Existing studies span connectome-constrained modeling, spiking graph neural networks, local learning rules, and cognitive representations, but differ in their computational objectives and the evidence supporting their use in graph learning. This review examines these studies through four related dimensions: structure, dynamics, plasticity, and cognition. We first establish the theoretical foundations and distinguish brain-inspired computational mechanisms from the use of brain-derived graph data. We then analyze how neural connectivity principles shape graph organization and information propagation, how neuronal dynamics support temporal state processing, and how plasticity and cognitive mechanisms contribute to adaptation, memory, and relational reasoning. Representative studies are compared in terms of their computational mechanisms, application settings, and limitations, with attention to the distinction between direct graph-learning evidence and findings from neural or cognitive modeling. We further discuss the tasks, benchmark datasets, evaluation measures, and implementation costs relevant to assessing these approaches. Finally, we summarize unresolved issues in relating neural principles to graph computation, coordinating structural and temporal processes, maintaining knowledge under graph changes, and scaling spiking implementations. This review provides a mechanism-oriented account of current research and identifies the computational questions that remain open in brain-inspired graph learning.

articles.title: Semantic-Topological Cognitive Maps for Assistive Indoor Navigation of a Robot Partner
articles.authors: Anhar Risnumawan, Achmad Fahrul Aji, Raditya Artha Rochmanto
articles.venue: Journal of Advanced Computational Intelligence and Intelligent Informatics
articles.abstract: Assistive indoor mobile robots are increasingly expected to connect natural-language requests about familiar places and objects with the metric maps used for localization and motion planning. Metric simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) supports reliable geometry and collision avoidance, whereas many open-vocabulary scene-graph systems remain separated from the navigation stacks used on deployed robots. This paper presents a semantic-topological cognitive map (STCM) that bridges these representations for assistive navigation. The system derives place nodes from a LiDAR–inertial pose stream through a dual growing neural gas backend and consolidates object instances over time. GroundingDINO and MobileSAM provide open-vocabulary semantic grounding in the map frame through LiDAR–image association and temporal score fusion. A tool-mediated large language model interface maps user commands to explicit STCM nodes, while graph search and ROS 2 Navigation2 (Nav2) remain responsible for path computation and execution. Evaluation with recorded robot sessions, an outdoor distribution-shift probe, and a public indoor-scene benchmark indicates that the STCM backend improves object-graph construction and that the language interface improves functional-command grounding when requested objects are recoverable by perception. The pipeline is demonstrated on a Ranger Garden Assistant platform with FAST-LIO2 mapping, incremental graph construction during the mapping pass, and waypoint execution from a serialized map artifact.

articles.title: Reactive, subjective and executive agents: How survival circuits underlie the expansion of subjective experience and felt motivation in humans and other vertebrates.
articles.authors: Giske J, Budaev S, Eliassen S, Mangel M, McNamara JM, Okasha S, Jørgensen C.
articles.abstract: We review the evolution of agency in vertebrates from the Cambrian explosion to humans. Active locomotion sparked evolution of efficient decision-making in arthropods, vertebrates and later in cephalopods. Isolated neural pathways-ancient control architectures for fitness-effective action-became interconnected survival circuits: evolutionarily conserved, functionally integrated neural pathways responding to specific classes of stimuli and that compete for control, with their own set of specific responses. Computational complexity was reduced by constraining inputs, processing and outputs. We hypothesize that three evolutionary transitions deepened the subjective experience by extending the survival circuits: (i) Associative and social learning implied non-genetic information acquisition; (ii) A simulated reality where episodic-like memory and internal simulation resulted in prediction-based action-selection; (iii) Setting and executing one's own wellbeing goals based on future expectations produced a felt experience of short-term personal goals. This subjective agency in vertebrates and some arthropods and cephalopods evolved from reactive agency. Key to this transition was the mighty quadruple-subjective experience, social learning, simulation-based prediction and felt goals-paving the way for nonverbal rationality and consciousness, again reinforcing each other. The emergence of culture, social bonding and the beginning of friendship started in early vertebrates. In humans and partly in some other lineages, the mighty quadruple coevolved with language-based culture under adaptation to social games into executive agency, enhancing the capacities for friendship and sociability and the impact of personalised and conscious norms, values and purpose in the survival circuits, further strengthening the feeling of free will.
